skill.name: The dilemma: what a character wants and what stands in the way
skill.why: Every story is someone wanting something, with something in the way.
skill.how: Ask what the character wants most. Then ask what is stopping them.

beats.say: Most stories start with someone who wants something.
beats.show: Mo **wants to win the island cook-off**.

beats.say: Then something gets in the way.
beats.show: But **his oven is full of seagulls**.

beats.say: The want plus the problem. That's the dilemma.
Sometimes the problem is another want.
beats.show: Mo **wants the trophy**, but he **also wants to help his mate**.

beats.say: So ask: what do they want? What's stopping them?

weDo.prompt: Which sentence sums up Hana's dilemma?
weDo.hint: What has Hana saved for? Who else could use that money?
weDo.success: Her skateboard money could buy her brother's game instead. Two wants pull against each other.

options.reason: Nothing says the shop sold out. Her money could go to her brother instead.

options.text: She wants a skateboard, but she also wants to cheer up her brother.

encounters.text: Every year, the Twotide lighthouse held a sleepover for kids who were brave enough. Ethan's big sister had stayed the whole night when she was ten. She still talked about it at every family dinner. 'Ten whole hours,' she would say. 'Not one peek outside.' Ethan was ten now. He packed a pillow, two blankets and a cheese sandwich. He didn't care about ghosts. He didn't even like torches. But he wanted to come home in the morning and say, 'I stayed the whole night too.' At midnight, the lighthouse made a long, creaking moan. encounters.text: The poster was stuck to every lamppost on Twotide Atoll: REWARD! $10,000 FOR A LIVE GLOWFIN, DELIVERED TO MAXX VANTABLACK'S ECHO STUDIO. Under it was a photo of Maxx, winking at the camera with his thumbs up. Marisol had read it eleven times, because two days ago, in the rock pool behind her house, she had found a Glowfin. It was smaller than her hand and shimmered blue whenever she sang to it. Ten thousand dollars would fix the hole in her dad's fishing boat, which had sat on the beach since the cyclone. Without the boat, her dad had no work, and Marisol had heard her parents whispering late at night about selling the house. Her little brother had already spent the money in his head, on a trampoline, a puppy and a lifetime supply of ice blocks. But she had also watched Maxx's streams. She had seen the 'rescued' Creatures in their tiny gold tanks, never shimmering at all. That night, she sat by the rock pool with a bucket in her lap for nearly an hour. The Glowfin swam in slow circles, glowing every time she hummed. Twice she lowered the bucket into the water, and twice she lifted it out again, empty.

parts: Every run went the same way. She would fly through the first nine levels, faster than FrogQueen had ever gone, with her heart pounding in her ears. Then she would reach the Triple Lava Jump, and her frog would sizzle. At midnight, on her four hundred and first try, she took a deep breath, wiggled her fingers and pressed start. Her mum had long ago stopped asking what all the screaming was about, and her cat, who had watched every attempt, put its paws over its eyes.

encounters.frame: Gus is reading about an inventor with a robot and a long list of problems. The Dashling is reading the list.
encounters.text: Ada had built a robot that could sort recycling faster than any machine on Twotide Atoll. It picked out bottles, cans and cardboard with its spindly arms and dropped them into the right bins, humming a little tune as it worked. Her teacher said it was good enough for the National Young Inventors Fair in the city, and Ada wanted, more than anything, to stand beside it there. Getting there would not be simple. The entry fee was two hundred dollars, and Ada had saved forty-three. The rules said every entry needed a team of two, but Ada couldn't bear the thought of anyone else touching her robot, not even her best friend. The robot's battery died after three minutes, and each demonstration lasted five. Worst of all, the fair ended with every inventor explaining their work to a panel of judges, and Ada froze whenever she had to speak to adults she didn't know. The last time a teacher had asked her a question in front of the class, she had answered in a whisper and then hidden in the library for the rest of lunch. Entries closed in a fortnight. Ada stuck a list of her problems on the fridge and stared at it every morning over her cereal.
encounters.prompt: Match each thing in Ada's way to where the problem comes from.
encounters.success: Some problems are rules, money and batteries. Others, like her fear and not sharing, come from inside Ada herself.

encounters.frame: Gus wrote a note about the smelliest news story of the year. One word is wrong.
encounters.text: TWOTIDE TIMES. A plant known as the corpse flower has become the most talked-about resident of Twotide Atoll, and it hasn't even opened yet. The giant flower, which stands taller than a grown man, blooms only once every seven years, and when it does, it gives off a smell that one gardener described as 'a dead possum wearing old socks'. Botanist Professor Pippa Gale has waited seven years for this bloom. She wants scientists from around the world to study it, because nobody has ever recorded how the smell changes hour by hour. 'This could be the most important week of my career,' she said. Unfortunately, the flower's neighbours do not agree. After complaints from the café next door, which says customers have been fainting into their soup, the island council has voted to dig the plant up and put it through the mulcher on Friday. The flower is expected to bloom on Sunday. Professor Gale has started a petition, chained herself to the greenhouse door, and offered to buy the café owner a peg for his nose. So far, the council has not changed its mind, although one councillor admitted she was 'a little bit curious about the smell'.

encounters.frame: Mo is telling the crew about his grandma's birthday. The Dashling has spotted the balloons.
encounters.text: 'I don't want a fuss,' Grandma Joy announced in March, three months before her eightieth birthday. 'No party. No cake. Just a quiet cup of tea.' She said it again in April, and twice in May. Yet strange things kept happening. In April, she left a magazine open on the kitchen table at an article called 'Ten Fabulous Party Ideas', with three of them circled in red pen. She casually mentioned that the surf club hall was free on the Saturday of her birthday, and that it held a hundred people. When the family asked what she wanted as a present, she said 'nothing', then added that a disco ball might be nice for the kitchen. She bought a silver sequinned dress, 'for no reason at all'. Mum found a list in Grandma's handbag titled PEOPLE I WOULDN'T MIND SEEING, with sixty-four names on it, including the man who had delivered her mail forty years ago. When Grandpa suggested they just go out for fish and chips, Grandma Joy went very quiet and ate her dinner without a word. The whole family held an emergency meeting in the garage. 'She says she doesn't want a party,' said Uncle Theo. Everybody looked at him. 'Theo,' said Mum gently, 'she has already ordered the balloons.'
encounters.prompt: What does Grandma Joy really want?
encounters.success: A big party. Her words say no fuss, but her actions, like the guest list and balloons, say otherwise.

encounters.frame: Narra the Teller is telling the story of the Twotide lighthouse ghost. The Dashling feels sorry for him.
encounters.text: For two hundred years, the ghost of Captain Horace Bleak had haunted Twotide lighthouse in perfect peace. Nobody visited. The stairs creaked, the wind howled, and Horace spent his evenings drifting from room to room, which was exactly how he liked it. Then, last spring, Maxx Vantablack arrived with three drones and a ring light to film a 'Midnight Ghost Hunt' for his channel. Horace, deeply annoyed, rattled a chain and moaned until Maxx screamed, tripped over his own cape and fled down the stairs. The clip was watched forty million times. Now coachloads of tourists arrived every night, waving selfie sticks and shouting, 'Do the chain thing!' Horace tried to get rid of them. He slammed doors, made the lamps flicker and wailed so loudly that a tour guide fainted. Every single time, the visitors cheered, filmed it and posted it online, and every single time, even more of them came the next night. A souvenir shop opened at the bottom of the hill, selling plastic chains and T-shirts that said I GOT BLEAKED. On Tuesday, someone gave Horace a five-star review on a travel website. Horace sat at the top of the lighthouse with his head in his hands, wondering whether a ghost was allowed to move house.

encounters.success: His scaring backfires. Every fright gets filmed, so every scare brings even more visitors.
